text: And the place filled up fast.
In 1880 the township counted about 15,700 people.
By the end of the decade it held roughly 85,000.
That is more than a fivefold jump in nine years, the kind of growth that strains everything a small government can provide.
A town that size needs water it can trust, sewers that actually work, and police and fire it can staff and pay for.

After the lessons of the great fire of 1871, a reliable water supply for fighting fires was not a small matter, and a township government built for a few thousand farmers and resort-goers was straining to provide it.
Hyde Park could not easily build all of that on its own.
Chicago could, and Chicago was right next door, hungry to grow.
So on June 29th, 1889, the question went to a vote, and Hyde Park Township chose to join the city of Chicago.
It was part of the largest single annexation in the city's history.
In one day Chicago took in around 125 square miles and about 225,000 people, and Hyde Park was the prize at the center of it.
The vote was, in plain terms, a trade.
The township handed over its independence and got the city's water mains, its sewer lines, and its fire and police protection in return.
Not everyone wanted it, and the question of self-rule against city services was argued hard, but the majority decided the city could simply do what a small township no longer could.
Cornell's lakefront bet had paid off so completely that the suburb dissolved into the very metropolis it had been built to give people an escape from.
